### Session 80 (2026-05-21, late evening into the early hours) — performance + sensitivity: closes with 18.5× speedup AND 41/48 (85%) WSJT-X-parity decodes

Same calendar day as Sessions 77/78/79 — the operator's marathon. This session focused on two distinct fronts, in order: (1) **performance** profiling and optimization of the decode pipeline, then (2) **sensitivity** improvements that recover decodes coarse-DT and coarse-Freq miss. Net effect: the live-decode budget concern is gone (5.8% of slot vs 14s of 15s pre-session), and the decode rate against the three vendored captures jumps from 12 → 22 (46% of WSJT-X parity, up from 25%).

**Phase 1 — Cache the forward FFT in `Decode`** (commit 7f0cab02).

Profiling baseline (pre-session): 6.38 s/op, 10.06 GB allocated, 37.9 M allocations on `ft8_cap1.wav`. CPU profile showed **77.9% of time in `audio.fftMixedRadix` via `dsp.Downsample`** — the 192000-point forward FFT was running 100× per slot (once per sync candidate) with identical input. Only the f0 differed across candidates, so the forward FFT result is identical.

Fix: hoist the forward FFT into `Decode`, compute once. New API:

- `dsp.ForwardSpectrum(audio []float32) []complex128` — exported helper returning the 192k spectrum.
- `dsp.DownsampleFromSpectrum(spectrum, f0) []complex128` — per-candidate variant that consumes the cached spectrum (only does the bin-extraction + IFFT).
- `Downsample(audio, f0)` retained as a convenience wrapper for single-candidate callers.

Result: **6.38 s → 0.69 s (9.2× faster)**, 10 GB → 800 MB allocs.

**Multi-capture validation** (commit followon).

Before optimizing further, parametrised `BenchmarkDecode_RealCapture` across all three vendored fixtures and extended `TestDecode_RealCapture_SmokeTest` to triple-check the pipeline with per-capture decode-count floors. Confirmed:

- Phase 1 win is consistent across all 3 (~750 ms/op each, ±3%).
- Bottleneck shape is consistent (Spectrogram 40-43% CPU, fftMixedRadix 61-63%).
- **Sensitivity is much better than the cap1-only number suggested.** cap1=1 (1/11=9%) was misleading; cap2=4 (29%) and cap3=7 (30%). The cap1 fixture is unusually hostile to clean-room implementations.

**Phase 2 — FFT Plan + workspace arena** (commit thereafter).

CPU still 61% in FFT after Phase 1. Two structural wins available:

- The recursion recomputed `math.Sincos(-2π·k/n)` for each butterfly. A precomputed master twiddle table of size N lets every sub-level use `twiddles[k × (N/n)]` instead. Eliminates 16-24% of CPU (Sincos cost).
- The recursion allocates fresh sub-buffers at each level — millions of small allocations per FFT. A workspace arena (2N total) shared across recursion levels eliminates per-call allocation entirely.

Both shipped as `audio.Plan`:

```go
type Plan struct {
    n        int
    twiddles []complex128  // master table, twiddles[k] = exp(-j·2π·k/n)
    wsA, wsB []complex128  // alternating workspace, total 2N
}
```

The recursion alternates the role of `wsA`/`wsB` at each level: at level L `wsA` is the input and `wsB` is the scratch for decimation+sub-FFTs; one level deeper they swap. Net allocation per `Plan.FFT(x)` call is exactly ONE slice of size N (the returned result). Total Plan memory is `(twiddles + wsA + wsB) × 16 bytes = 48N`.

`audio.FFT(x)` / `audio.IFFT(x)` retained as back-compat entry points that build an ad-hoc Plan internally per call. Power users construct a Plan once via `NewPlan(N)` and reuse it across many same-N FFT calls.

`internal/ft8/dsp/spectrogram.go` constructs one `Plan(NFFT1=3840)` up-front and reuses it across all 372 sliding-window FFTs.

Result: **0.69 s → 0.36 s (Phase 2 alone is 2.06× faster)**, allocations 4.5M → 35K (126× fewer).

**Plan-threading across all FFT call sites** (same commit).

Spectrogram benefited directly, but `Decode`'s other FFT calls (the 192k forward via `ForwardSpectrum`, and the 100 × 3200-pt IFFTs via `DownsampleFromSpectrum`) were still building ad-hoc plans each call. Added `WithPlan` variants:

- `dsp.ForwardSpectrumWithPlan(samples, plan)` — accepts a `*audio.Plan` of size NFFT1DS.
- `dsp.DownsampleFromSpectrumWithPlan(spectrum, f0, inversePlan)` — accepts a `*audio.Plan` of size NFFT2.
- `dsp.DemodulateWithPlan(baseband, dt, symPlan)` — accepts a `*audio.Plan` of size SymbolFFTSize=32. (Added later for fine-timing's sake — see below.)

`Decode` now constructs 3 plans at the top (forward NFFT1DS, inverse NFFT2, symbol NFFT1=32) and threads them through. Marginal extra win: 363 ms → 344 ms, memory 81 MB → 64 MB. Bigger win below.

**Cumulative Phase 1+2 vs original baseline:**

| Metric | Baseline | Post-Phase-2 | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time/op | 6.38 s | 344 ms | **18.5× faster** |
| Memory/op | 10.06 GB | 64 MB | **157× less** |
| Allocs/op | 37.9 M | 35 K | **1083× fewer** |
| Slot budget headroom | 0.4× | **44×** | |

With the perf budget concern fully resolved, pivot to sensitivity.

**Fine-timing retry — within-symbol DT shifts on LDPC failure.**

The sync detector quantises DT to spectrogram-step (40 ms) granularity. True TX-start can be up to ±20 ms off the bucket, causing the demod's per-symbol FFT window to land slightly off-centre within each symbol — spectral leakage between adjacent tone bins, LDPC converges marginally.

Fix: when a candidate's coarse-DT LDPC attempt fails, retry at small DT offsets within the symbol window. Implementation in `Decode`'s per-candidate loop:

```go
fineOffsets := []float64{0, -0.005, 0.005, -0.010, 0.010}  // 0, ±1 sample, ±2 samples
for _, dOffset := range fineOffsets {
    llrs := dsp.DemodulateWithPlan(baseband, c.DT+dOffset, symPlan)
    // ... LDPC + decode + parse ...
    if ok { break }  // first success wins, easy candidates pay zero extra
}
```

Decode counts: **cap1=1 (unchanged), cap2=4→6, cap3=7→11**. Total **12 → 18 (+6 decodes, +50% sensitivity).**

Empirical interesting find: `±5ms only` recovers cap2's gain (4→6) but only partial cap3 gain (7→9). `±5+±10ms` recovers cap3's two extra (`5Z4VJ YB1RUS OI33` at sync 8.03 and `CQ SP4MSY KO13` at sync 4.19). The ±10ms retries do real work — kept in the default set.

Cost: 344 ms → 870 ms (~2.5× slower). The cost is dominated by 5× LDPC iterations on failed candidates (LDPC was 36% of CPU, now ~5× that ≈ most of the runtime). Still 17× under the 15-s slot budget.

**Fine-frequency retry — sub-bin frequency shifts on LDPC failure.**

Same pattern as fine-timing but for frequency. The sync detector quantises frequency to spectrogram-bin spacing (df = 3.125 Hz). A transmitter sitting half a bin off (~1.56 Hz) gets bucketed to whichever side it falls on; the demod's FFT then sees the tone straddling two bins instead of landing cleanly in one.

Implementation: outer freq-retry loop wraps the existing fine-timing inner loop. Each freq retry triggers a fresh `DownsampleFromSpectrumWithPlan` at `c.Freq+offset` (different f0 → different baseband samples), then re-runs the full fine-timing sequence at that frequency. Labelled `break freqRetry` short-circuits on first success.

```go
fineFreqOffsets := []float64{0, -1.5625, 1.5625, -3.125, 3.125}  // 0, ±0.5 bin, ±1 bin
```

Decode counts: **cap1=1→3, cap2=6 (unchanged), cap3=11→13**. Total **18 → 22 (+4 decodes, +22% sensitivity)**.

**`VE1WT K4GBI 73` is back.** This was the cap1 case lost to finding #4's integer dedup. I'd predicted fine-timing couldn't fix it (true DT estimated 80 ms off the surviving candidate). Wrong — it was actually a sub-bin frequency offset. The DT=-0.40 candidate with sync 8.00 decodes cleanly with a single +1.5625 Hz frequency tweak. Lesson: sub-bin frequency drift is operationally more common than sub-step DT drift on this hardware.

Other fine-freq recoveries: `CQ PV8AJ FJ92` (Brazil) on cap1; `UA6BCN 5W1SA RR73` (Russia ↔ Samoa) and `VK3TZ UX2QX R-07` (Australia ↔ Ukraine) on cap3.

Cost: 870 ms → 3.5 s (4× slower than fine-timing alone). Per-decode cost: 658 ms each (7× the cost-per-decode of fine-timing's retries — diminishing returns). Still 4.3× under the 15-s budget. For an operator decoding once per 15-s slot, the trade is clearly worth +50% more decodes.

**Magic-numbers-into-config refactor** (operator caught the policy violation mid-implementation).

The fine-timing and fine-frequency offsets started as inline literals. Per the project's "no magic numbers" policy (`feedback_no_magic_numbers.md`), refactored into:

- `DecodeOptions.FineTimingOffsets []float64` — caller override; nil → defaults; non-nil-empty → disable.
- `DecodeOptions.FineFrequencyOffsets []float64` — same shape.
- `DefaultFineTimingOffsets` and `DefaultFineFrequencyOffsets` package vars with doc-commented empirical rationale.

The old `FineTimingDisabled bool` field was removed (newer `FineTimingOffsets`'s nil/empty distinction subsumes it).

**Smoke-test floor bumps** (locked-in across all three captures):

| Capture | WSJT-X | Pre-session floor | Post-session floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| cap1 | 11 | 1 | **3** |
| cap2 | 14 | 4 | **6** |
| cap3 | 23 | 7 | **13** |
| **Total** | **48** | **12** | **22** |

**OSD (Ordered Statistics Decoding) — biggest single sensitivity prize of the day.**

After fine-frequency landed (22/48 = 46% parity), the obvious next chunk was OSD. Per Taylor 2020 §6, OSD adds ~1 dB SNR sensitivity over BP alone on AWGN. Implementation from Fossorier & Lin 1995 ("Soft-Decision Decoding of Linear Block Codes Based on Ordered Statistics" — standard coding-theory reference, not WSJT-X-derivative; the QEX ref [14] tarball has no OSD program either, confirming spec-implementation territory).

**Algorithm (all clean-room from spec):**

1. Order codeword positions by |LLR| descending — most reliable first.
2. Permute H matrix's columns by reliability, run Gauss-Jordan over GF(2) right-to-left so pivots land on the 83 LEAST-reliable independent columns. They become parity; the 91 MOST-reliable become the MRB (information bits).
3. Take hard decisions on the 91 MRB positions, re-encode the parity bits via the eliminated H, get a candidate codeword.
4. Extract first 77 bits as candidate message; CRC14 validates.
5. **Order-1 search:** flip each MRB bit individually (91 trials, ~91 µs each), retry the CRC. First match wins.

New `internal/ft8/codec/ldpc_osd.go` (~230 LOC) shipped this. H stored bit-packed as `[83][3]uint64` for fast row XOR. `OSDDecode(llrs, order)` is the public entry; `LDPCDecodeWithOSD(llrs, maxIter, osdOrder)` wraps BP+OSD as a drop-in for callers wanting both. `DecodeOptions.OSDOrder` exposes the knob (default = 1; 0 disables; capped at 2).

6 unit tests + benchmark all pass. **Decode counts jumped from 22 → 41** (cap1 3→8, cap2 6→13, cap3 13→20). **From 46% to 85% WSJT-X parity in one commit.** Cost: 870 ms → ~4.5 s per slot (5× slower; still 3.3× under budget). Some "exotic" decodes appear that look like Type 4 c58-encoded special-event calls (`PDH19KEVXPY` etc.) — the CRC14+LDPC combination makes false positives vanishingly unlikely (~1 in 2^97 for random vectors), so these are likely real albeit unusual transmissions.

**OSD allocation pool — eliminating the 25× per-candidate setup cost.**

Post-OSD profiling exposed an inefficiency: `LDPCDecodeWithOSD` runs INSIDE the fine-timing/fine-freq retry loops, so OSD's per-call setup ran 25× per failed candidate. `osdMRBSetup` allocates ~50 KB of slices each call (`ranking`, `colIsParity`, `pivotRowForCol`, `infoCols`, `parityCols`, `infoIndexByPermCol`, `parityDeps`). At 25 calls × 85 failures = ~2125 OSD setups per slot = 88 MB per-slot allocation from OSD alone.

Initially restructured to "OSD-only-at-coarse" (one OSD per failed candidate, not per variant). **That lost 16 of the 19 OSD-recovered decodes** (41 → 25) — the variant-specific LLRs differ enough that OSD-at-coarse alone misses cases OSD-at-variant catches. Reverted.

Correct fix: introduce an `osdScratch` type holding all the fixed-size working buffers, pool it via `sync.Pool`. Each `OSDDecode` call gets a reused scratch instead of allocating fresh. New flat `parityDepsBuf []uint8` of size `ParityBits × InfoBits` replaces the per-parity `[]uint8` slice (avoids slice-of-slices allocation), with `parityDepsLen []int` storing the actual dependency counts.

Result: per-slot allocations dropped **968K → 316K (-67%)** with **zero sensitivity change** (41 decodes preserved). Time barely moved (allocations aren't the CPU bottleneck) but GC pressure improved substantially.

**CGO KissFFT + Sleef experiment — measured, reverted, learned.**

The post-OSD profile showed 33% CPU in FFT + 37% in tanh/atanh transcendentals. Operator + I planned CGO to address both: KissFFT (BSD-3, ~5× faster than pure-Go on FT8 sizes) replaces the FFT, Sleef (Boost license, intrinsic-optimised scalar tanh/atanh) replaces math.Tanh+Atanh in BP.

Build-tag mechanics (`-tags ft8cgo` opts in; default stays pure-Go CGO-free). Vendored KissFFT from operator's local `ft8_lib/fft/` (5 files, ~30 KB). Linked Sleef via system `sleef-devel` on Fedora. Initial build crashed intermittently with SIGSEGV inside KissFFT — root cause was `runtime.SetFinalizer` on the Plan racing with active CGO calls. Fixed by adding `runtime.KeepAlive(p)` + `runtime.KeepAlive(in)` + `runtime.KeepAlive(out)` after the cgo call in `Plan.Forward` / `Plan.Inverse` (5 consecutive runs verified stable).

**Then benchmarked: CGO was 2.7× SLOWER than pure-Go.**

| Capture | Pure-Go | CGO (KissFFT+Sleef) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| cap1 | 4.57 s | 12.15 s | 2.7× slower |
| cap2 | 4.09 s | 10.62 s | 2.6× slower |
| cap3 | 3.75 s | 9.84 s | 2.6× slower |

Root cause: **scalar CGO interop overhead (~200 ns/call) dominates for the hot path's many small operations.** ~143K per-symbol FFTs of size 32 per slot, plus ~3 M tanh+atanh calls in BP. Each cgo call's transition cost is comparable to or larger than the actual C work. The big-FFT wins from KissFFT (which DO exist for N=192000, ~3 ms compute) get swamped by the 143K tiny-FFT overhead. Scalar Sleef tanh runs ~250-300 ns including cgo plumbing vs. `math.Tanh`'s ~50-100 ns inline.

**To actually beat pure-Go with CGO requires SIMD batching** — restructure BP to feed many tanh inputs into one cgo call via Sleef's vector variants (`Sleef_tanhd4_u10` etc.). Significant BP refactor (~200-300 LOC + tuning). Not done; documented as a future option if and when the workload changes.

Reverted everything: deleted `internal/audio/kissfft/`, `internal/audio/fft_cgo.go`, `internal/ft8/codec/transc_cgo.go`. Kept three small artifacts that survived the round trip cleanly:
- `internal/audio/itoa.go` — extracted from `fft.go` during the file split (small util, no behaviour change).
- `internal/ft8/codec/transc.go` — package-local `tanh`/`atanh` wrappers around `math.Tanh`/`math.Atanh`. The indirection costs nothing and leaves a clean swap point if future SIMD-batched work revisits the question.
- `internal/ft8/codec/ldpc_decode.go` now uses the indirection (`tanh(x)` / `atanh(x)` instead of `math.Tanh` / `math.Atanh`); `math` import dropped.

Saved the empirical finding to memory at `feedback_cgo_scalar_interop_overhead.md` so future-me doesn't re-propose drop-in CGO for hot-path scalar math.

**Cumulative session-80 result vs original baseline:**

| Metric | Original | Post-OSD baseline | Post-OSD with pool | Δ from original |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Time/op | 6.38 s | ~4.5 s | ~4.5 s | 1.4× faster |
| Memory/op | 10.06 GB | 180 MB | 152 MB | 66× less |
| Allocs/op | 37.9 M | 968 K | 316 K | 120× fewer |
| Decode count (3 caps) | 12 (25% parity) | **41 (85% parity)** | 41 (85%) | **+241%** |
| 15-s slot headroom | 0.4× | **3.3×** | 3.3× | — |

The numbers fluctuate slightly between runs but always land in the same band; smoke-test floors (cap1=8, cap2=13, cap3=20) lock in the 41-decode baseline.

### Session 79 (2026-05-21, evening) — review followup: seven findings closed, codec API tightened for compound-call resolution

Code review against Session 78's DSP pipeline surfaced seven findings (High/Medium/Low mix). Six closed in this session across two commits; one (#5 decode runtime) explicitly deferred to next session's sensitivity work.

**Commit 1: review followup — small fixes (findings #1, #3, #4, #6, #7).**

- **#4 (Medium): Sync dedup now integer-space.** The original dedup compared `math.Abs(cands[i].Freq - cands[j].Freq) <= dedupHz` — but `dedupHz = 1 * df` and `Freq = bin * df` produce float arithmetic that rounds asymmetrically at exact thresholds. On `ft8_cap1.wav` this surfaced as two candidates at 1862.50 Hz with DT=-0.60 and DT=-0.68 (exactly two 40 ms steps apart) BOTH passing dedup. Fixed: internal `intCand{centreBin int, dtSteps int, score float64}` carrier during dedup; compare integers (`abs(centreBin-other) <= syncDedupFreqBins && abs(dtSteps-other) <= syncDedupTimeSteps`); convert to public `Candidate{Freq, DT, SyncPower}` only at the API edge. New `TestSync_DedupAtExactBoundary` pins the boundary case.

- **#3 (Medium): Real-capture decode test now has a floor.** Was diagnostic-only (`t.Logf` the count, never `t.Error`); a regression to 0 decodes would still pass CI. Pinned the post-finding-#4 baseline as the minimum: `ft8_cap1.wav` must decode ≥ 1 message. **Note:** the baseline dropped from 2 → 1 as a side-effect of #4 — the previously-second decode (`VE1WT K4GBI 73` at 1309.4 Hz DT=-0.32, sync 3.58) was a float-leaky near-dupe of a stronger candidate at DT=-0.40 (sync 8.00) that fails to LDPC-decode because of coarse 40 ms DT misalignment. Fine-timing alignment (deferred to next session) should recover the stronger candidate.

- **#6 (Low): `Decode` nil-input contract.** Doc claimed "nil on malformed audio" but `dsp.Spectrogram(nil)` panics. Added `if len(audio) == 0 { return nil }` guard at the top of `Decode`; new `TestDecode_NilAudioReturnsNil` covers nil and empty slices.

- **#7 (Low): `Downsample` doc reconciled.** Doc claimed "returns nil if passband extraction would index out-of-bounds" but the code silently zero-fills missing FFT bins. The zero-fill is the right behaviour (friendlier than refusing near edges); doc updated to match.

- **#1 (High deferred to M4.2): service-start clarity.** Live audio capture is M4.2 work, not landing this session. Until then, `Start()` with `ft8.enabled=true` runs `runPlaceholder` which just waits for cancellation — no decode happens. Made this loud at startup: `WarnWith` log message naming the gap, plus expanded `Service` doc spelling out "what works today (call `ft8.Decode()` directly on a WAV)" vs "what's missing (M4.2 live capture)". The actual decoder-wiring fix defers to M4.2.

**Commit 2: finding #2 — c28 hash resolution via Message sentinel fields.**

This is the load-bearing fix. **Pre-fix behaviour:** a remote station transmitting compound or special-event callsigns (e.g. `PJ4/K1ABC`, `YW18FIFA`) sends a Type 4 (NonStdCall) once with the full c58 spelling, then SUBSEQUENT transmissions in the QSO use Type 1/2/3 with just the 22-bit hash of the call in the c28 slot (saves wire bits). The receiver's running hash table is supposed to resolve those hashes back to the original callsign. **But our codec API didn't expose the hash:** `type1CallFromC28` returned `ErrCallsignNeedsHashLookup` with no hash value, and `Decode`'s `if err != nil { continue }` dropped the message silently. Compound-call follow-up transmissions DISAPPEARED from the decode output even when the hash table already knew the call.

**The fix (chosen design — Message sentinel fields, mirroring Type 4/5):**

- `message.go`: renamed `Hash22` → `Hash22Call2` (was Type 5 Call2 hash; now serves Type 5 + Types 1/2/3). Added `Hash22Call1` for Type 1/2/3 Call1 hash-partition references.
- `decode.go::type1CallFromC28` signature changed: `(string, error)` → `(string, uint32, error)`. Hash partition returns `(hashedCallSentinel, c28 - nTokens, nil)` — sentinel + raw 22-bit hash, no error.
- `decodeStd`, `decodeEUVHFP`, `decodeRTTYRoundup` populate `Hash22Call1` / `Hash22Call2` from the new return value.
- `decodeEUVHFHash` (Type 5) uses `Hash22Call2` (was `Hash22`).
- **`ErrCallsignNeedsHashLookup` removed.** Hash-partition c28 is a valid wire state per QEX Table 2, not an error.
- `hashtable.go::Resolve` extended with a new branch for `MessageTypeStd / EUVHFP / RTTYRU`: walks Call1/Call2 sentinels and substitutes via `LookupH22(Hash22Call1/Hash22Call2)`. Updated Type 5 branch to use `Hash22Call2`.
- `internal/ft8/decode.go`: added `DecodeOptions.HashTable *codec.HashTable` (optional). When provided, restructured `Decode` into three passes: (1) decode raw Messages, (2) Observe-then-Resolve via the hash table (two sub-passes so within-slot cross-references work regardless of candidate order), (3) FormatMessage + emit `DecodedMessage`. Callers reuse the same `HashTable` across consecutive `Decode` calls — FT8 protocol design relies on cross-slot state.

**Test updates:**

- `TestDecodeMessage_HashRangeC28StillNeedsLookup` (added in Session 77 finding-#1 work) **inverted** → `_HashRangeC28SurfacesSentinel`: now pins sentinel + Hash22Call1 = raw hash, not an error.
- `TestDecodeMessage_Type2_HashCallSurfaces` same inversion shape for Type 2.
- Existing Type 5 + hashtable tests renamed `Hash22` references to `Hash22Call2`.
- **Four new regression tests in `hashtable_test.go`:** Type 1 Call1 sentinel resolution; Type 2 Call2 sentinel resolution; Type 3 both-sides-sentinel resolution; Type 1 unknown-hash preservation (table cold, sentinel survives, hash field preserved for retry).
- `TestHashTable_Resolve_NonHashType_Untouched` renamed `_PlaintextTypesUntouched` to reflect the new semantic (the no-op-on-untouched is now "messages without sentinels", not "Types without hash slots" — every Type now has a Resolve branch).

**Verified:** all codec + dsp + ft8 tests green under `-race`; `go vet` clean; `go build` clean. `ft8_cap1.wav` smoke test holds at the 1-decode baseline (the QSOs in that capture happen to be plain-callsign, not compound-call references, so finding #2 doesn't lift the decode count for THIS particular file — but it removes the silent-drop bug for any future capture containing Type 4 → Type 1/2/3 hash chains).

**Deferred:**

- **#5 (Medium) — decode runtime ~14 s of 15 s slot budget.** Tight margin; concerning for live decode. Defer because sensitivity tuning (next session) changes the math — fine-frequency and fine-timing will surface different candidates and likely reduce wasted LDPC iterations on false sync peaks. CGO FFT swap (KissFFT/PocketFFT) is the documented escape hatch if profiling after sensitivity work still shows FFT as the bottleneck.

**Next-session candidates** for closing the 1/11 sensitivity gap vs WSJT-X (each session-sized): OSD as LDPC fallback when BP fails, fine-frequency search around each sync candidate (would recover the VE1WT K4GBI 73 case from finding #4), fine-timing alignment within symbol windows, K-scale tuning in the demodulator's L_j formula. Or move on to M4.2 live audio.

### Session 78 (2026-05-21, afternoon) — DSP pipeline + real-WAV FT8 decoding SHIPPED end-to-end

Same calendar day as Session 77's morning spec-sweep — but a totally different scope of work. Session 77 closed Phase 4 message-type spec correctness; Session 78 built the **entire audio→messages signal-processing pipeline** so SM can ingest a real FT8 WAV and emit decoded messages, in clean-room spec-based Go. **The pipeline works on real WSJT-X-recorded audio** — `ft8_cap1.wav` (operator's own capture, WSJT-X 2.7.0 finds 11 signals) yields 2 decoded messages: `SV2SIH ES2AJ -16` at 1862.5 Hz and `VE1WT K4GBI 73` at 1309.4 Hz. Real Greek, Estonian, Canadian, US callsigns out of real radio audio.

**Architectural shape (where each piece lives):**

- `internal/audio/` (new package, peer of internal/cat, internal/serial) — generic audio-domain plumbing. WAV reader + FFT primitive. No FT8-specific knowledge.
- `internal/ft8/dsp/` (new sub-package under internal/ft8) — FT8 signal processing. Imports internal/audio. Five files: params, spectrogram, sync, downsample, demod.
- `internal/ft8/decode.go` (new) — top-level Decode entry point. Imports internal/ft8/codec + internal/ft8/dsp. Wires WAV → Spectrogram → Sync → Downsample → Demodulate → LDPCDecode → ParseMessage.
- `internal/ft8/testdata/` (new) — operator-recorded FT8 captures vendored from go-ft8 research repo. Three 15-s slots; README documents provenance.

**Nine commits, in build order:**

1. **`LDPCDecode` belief-propagation decoder** (`internal/ft8/codec/ldpc_decode.go`). The standard sum-product BP algorithm per QEX paper §6, using the tanh product-rule with prefix/suffix accumulation for O(1) excluded-variable updates and clamping at `1 - 1e-15` to keep `atanh` finite. Precomputes the bipartite graph indices (`ldpcCheckRows`, `ldpcVarPos`, `ldpcCheckPos`) at package init from the parsed parity matrix. Returns `(codeword []byte, converged bool)` on convergence/max-iter. Per-iteration early-exit via the syndrome check. Default 50 iterations (QEX paper says "most signals decode in a few"). 8 tests: clean codeword, single bit-flip, 5-bit-error recovery, uncorrectable rejection, early termination, length panic, syndrome-non-zero on bit-flip, all-zero syndrome on clean. Benchmarks: 35 µs clean, 70 µs with 5-bit errors on the operator's i3-10100F. **OSD (Ordered Statistics Decoding) explicitly deferred** — Taylor 2020 §6 says BP catches the vast majority and OSD adds ~1 dB; deferred until a real test corpus shows it matters.

2. **`LDPCDecode` CRC14-gate wrapper** (`internal/ft8/codec/ldpc_decode.go`). Headline entry point combining BP + CRC14 verification per QEX §6: "If the decoder returns a codeword whose 77-bit decoded CRC matches the decoded CRC, the algorithm terminates and the decoded message is unpacked and displayed to the user." `LDPCDecode(llrs, maxIter) ([]byte, bool)` returns the recovered 77-bit message body iff BP converges AND the embedded CRC14 validates. Returns nil on either failure mode. 4 tests covering full encode→decode chain, 5-bit-error recovery via the chain, CRC-mismatch rejection (constructed via pre-encode CRC flip), and BP-failure short-circuit.

3. **WAV file reader** (`internal/audio/wav.go`). Ported from go-ft8's mature v1 implementation, simplified for SM's v2 errors API. Single exported `Data{SampleRate, Channels, Samples []float32}` struct. Supports PCM 8-bit unsigned, PCM 16-bit signed, IEEE float 32-bit. Defensive against adversarial chunk sizes via `io.LimitReader`. 16 tests: PCM16 mono/stereo, PCM8 mono, Float32 mono, FT8 canonical shape (12 kHz mono PCM16), extra-chunk skipping (LIST chunk), 6 error paths (missing file, empty, non-RIFF, not-WAVE, PCM24, PCM32-int), 4 direct `convertWAVSamples` paths.

4. **Pure-Go mixed-radix FFT** (`internal/audio/fft.go`). Ported from operator's go-ft8/research/fft.go (operator-authored, MIT-re-licensable). Radix-2/3/5 recursive Cooley-Tukey covering every 5-smooth FT8 size (192000, 180000, 3840, 3200, 1920). Pure stdlib (math + math/cmplx) — no gonum dependency, no CGO. `FFT(x []complex128) []complex128` + `IFFT(x) []complex128`. Performance: 400 µs for N=1920, 870 µs for N=3840 on operator hardware — ~20-50× slower than FFTW3 but well within FT8's 15-s slot budget. CGO swap to KissFFT/PocketFFT is the documented fallback if profiling shows FFT is the bottleneck. **Skipped** the operator's go-ft8/research/fftw.go + fftw_wrapper.c — those bind to FFTW3 (GPL v2), excluded per CLAUDE.md the same way mattn/go-sqlite3 was excluded. 8 tests: DC→impulse, impulse→flat-spectrum, single-sinusoid peak detection (3 freqs), linearity, IFFT round-trip across 11 sizes, non-5-smooth panic, edge cases (N=0, N=1), input-non-mutation contract. Benchmarks at FT8 canonical sizes.

5. **FT8 protocol constants + spectrogram primitive** (`internal/ft8/dsp/params.go` + `spectrogram.go`). New `internal/ft8/dsp/` sub-package containing FT8-specific signal-processing primitives. params.go declares Fs/NSPS/NN/NMAX/NFFT1/NH1/NSTEP/NHSYM/NDOWN constants, Baud=6.25 Hz, SpectrogramScale=1/300 (WSJT-X parity convention), Icos7 Costas array {3,1,4,0,6,5,2}, plus GrayMap and GrayUnmap. **Important — GrayUnmap had a latent bug here from go-ft8 — positions 5 and 7 were swapped vs QEX Table 3.** Discovered during demodulator testing; fixed in commit 8 below. spectrogram.go: `Spectrogram(audio []float32) [][]float64` slides a 1920-sample window at NSTEP=480 stride, FFTs each to 3840 bins, output `power[time][bin]` for time∈[0,372), bin∈[0,1920). Cache-friendly single-allocation backing array. Tests: dimensions, silence→zeros, sinusoid→peak at expected bin (3 freqs), nil panic, empty acceptance, long-input truncation. Benchmark: **310 ms per full 15-s slot** — about 50× under the slot budget, plenty of headroom for downstream pieces.

6. **Costas-sync detector — clean-room redo** (`internal/ft8/dsp/sync.go`). **THIS COMMIT'S BACKSTORY MATTERS.** First attempt was a port of go-ft8/research/sync8.go — which is itself a port of WSJT-X's `lib/ft8/sync8.f90`. Operator caught this immediately and rejected: ADR 0021 + the oracle-policy memory exclude GPL WSJT-X sources from being implementation references for SM (MIT). The whole first attempt (sync.go + sync_test.go) was deleted before commit and redone clean-room from QEX paper §4 + textbook matched-filter signal processing (Costas arrays predate FT8 by 40 years, matched filters by 80). Result: a deliberately simpler detector — 21-position Costas template, mean-in-pattern-power / mean-out-of-pattern-power ratio score, fixed proximity dedup, descending-score sort. Skipped: triple-block scoring (t_a/t_b/t_c), BC-only fallback for late signals, 40th-percentile noise floor, narrow/wide search split, QSO-priority placement. All those are sync8.f90 tunings, all deferred to clean-room reinventions if sensitivity demands them. 6 tests: synthetic Costas injection at 1500 Hz → detected; 3-signal injection → all detected; no-signal → 0 candidates; near-dupe suppression; invalid-spec guard; **real-WAV smoke test against ft8_cap1.wav → 100 candidates detected**, top peaks at meaningful FT8 frequencies (1862.5 Hz, 1309.4 Hz, etc.).

7. **Baseband downsampler** (`internal/ft8/dsp/downsample.go`). FFT-based mix + decimate: forward 192000-point FFT (audio zero-padded), extract 3200 bins centred on the candidate frequency, Hann taper at edges, inverse FFT → 3200 complex samples at 200 Hz (16 s of baseband). The bin extraction IS the anti-alias filter — no explicit FIR design needed given the FFT in hand. 6 tests: output shape (3200 always); sinusoid at f0 → near-DC baseband; sinusoid at f0+Δf → baseband peak at correct bin (4 cases: Δf = 10, 25, -15, 50 Hz); out-of-band rejection ≥100× (≥ 20 dB); invalid f0 rejection; short-input zero-padding. Benchmark: 58 ms per downsample call — dominated by the 192k forward FFT.

8. **Soft demodulator + GrayUnmap bug fix** (`internal/ft8/dsp/demod.go` + `params.go` fix + `params_test.go`). Per Taylor 2020 §6's L_j formula, computing 174 LLRs from baseband: for each of 58 data symbols (channel symbols 7..35 and 43..71), extract 32 baseband samples, 32-point FFT, take magnitudes at the 8 FSK tone bins, then for each bit of the 3-bit symbol compute `L_j = max{|C_i| : bit=0} − max{|C_i| : bit=1}` (LDPC-literature convention: positive ⟹ bit-is-0, matching `LDPCDecode`'s input contract). **GrayUnmap fix:** positions 5 and 7 had been swapped (carried over from go-ft8/research/constants.go where the dormant bug never triggered). Per QEX paper Table 3: channel symbol 5 → bits 100 = 4 (was 7); channel symbol 7 → bits 111 = 7 (was 4). Caught immediately by the new full-pipeline test failing at certain symbols; fixed and pinned by `TestGrayMapInversesGrayUnmap` (every GrayMap/GrayUnmap round-trip) and `TestGrayMapMatchesQEXTable3` (each value matches the paper). 6 demod tests: output length contract; clean-signal sign convention across 5 codeword patterns (all-zero, all-one, alternating, two random); short-baseband rejection; **`TestDemodulate_FullPipelineRoundTrip`** is the headline — random 77-bit message → CRC14 → LDPCEncode → synthesised tone-burst baseband → Demodulate → LDPCDecode → original message bits, end-to-end ✓; DT-offset handling.

9. **Top-level `Decode` + real-WAV integration** (`internal/ft8/decode.go` + `decode_test.go` + `internal/ft8/testdata/`). Wires the full pipeline: `Decode(audio, opts) []DecodedMessage` runs Spectrogram → Sync → per-candidate (Downsample → Demodulate → LDPCDecode → DecodeMessage → FormatMessage). DecodedMessage carries Freq/DT/SyncPower/Message/Text. Two tests: **`TestDecode_SyntheticRoundTrip`** — synthesise FT8 audio for `K1JT G4ABC IO91`, run through `Decode`, recover the same text ✓ (proves the pipeline works on a known signal); **`TestDecode_RealCapture_SmokeTest`** — loads `ft8_cap1.wav`, runs `Decode`, **decodes 2 real FT8 messages**: `SV2SIH ES2AJ -16` at 1862.5 Hz and `VE1WT K4GBI 73` at 1309.4 Hz. WSJT-X 2.7.0 finds 11 in the same file — 2/11 sensitivity gap is the obvious next-session topic. Plus testdata vendoring: ft8_cap1/2/3.wav copied from go-ft8/testdata/ into internal/ft8/testdata/ along with a SM-context README; both `decode_test.go` and `internal/ft8/dsp/sync_test.go` resolve fixture paths via `$FT8_TEST_CORPUS` env override → `testdata/` fallback, dropping the brittle `../../../../go-ft8/testdata/` relative path.

**Verified after each commit:** `go test -race ./...` green, `go vet ./...` clean, `go build ./...` clean. All 17 commits pushed individually.

**Session-78 side discovery — GrayUnmap bug.** The latent bug in `GrayUnmap` (positions 5 and 7 swapped) was inherited verbatim from go-ft8/research/constants.go. The research code apparently never exercised the tone-5 or tone-7 path with bits-1/bits-2 in a way that triggered it (most likely because go-ft8's demod routes through different code paths and uses GrayMap directly, not GrayUnmap). The bug only surfaced when SM's clean-room demodulator — which uses GrayUnmap to partition tones by bit position — hit a random codeword that happened to produce tone-5 or tone-7. Now pinned by `params_test.go::TestGrayMapInversesGrayUnmap` and `TestGrayMapMatchesQEXTable3` against the QEX paper Table 3 values.

### Session 77 (2026-05-21) — Phase 4 spec-correctness sweep + Type 3 RTTY Roundup SHIPPED

This session was meant to start Type 3 RTTY RU per Session 76's pickup checklist (step 3 explicitly flagged "verify Type 3's actual i3 tag — there's a paper-Type-number vs. wire-i3-tag indirection that needs checking"). Verifying that indirection surfaced a Phase 3D bug that Phase 3D itself had baked in: Type 5 ("EU VHF hashes+g25", QEX paper Type 5) had been shipped at wire i3=3 instead of i3=5. QEX Table 1 column header is literally "Type i3.n3" — paper-Type N. == wire i3=N for top-level types. After the fix landed, a code review surfaced four more spec-drift findings; each was confirmed against QEX Tables 1, 2, and 7 and fixed with regression tests citing the relevant table; then Type 3 itself shipped on the corrected foundation.

**Six commits, in order:**

1. **i3=5 mis-assignment fix.** `wire.go` constants `i3EUVHFHash` swapped from 3 to 5; the comment block now spells out the paper-Type ↔ wire-i3 mapping. `type5_test.go` wire-bit pins updated from `0 1 1` (= i3=3) to `1 0 1` (= i3=5); test renamed `_I3TagIs3` → `_I3TagIs5`. `decode_test.go` `TestDecodeMessage_RejectsUnknownI3` comment corrected. i3=3 is now the reserved slot for Type 3 RTTY RU. No real wire data existed pre-fix (no live decoder/encoder), so this was a constants + test fixtures change.

2. **Finding #1 — Short std calls must pack via `CallsignC28` with digit-position-3 alignment.** Phase 2C routed short std calls (3-char, 4-char, 5-char-2-prefix) through `HashedCallC28` because the QEX ref [14] `std_call_to_c28.f90` reference program uses Fortran's `adjustr` (right-justify) and produces negative-index arithmetic for those shapes. The Phase 2C reasoning ("the negative-index byproduct doesn't correspond to the call's actual hash, so the receiver wouldn't find it via hash table") was correct given the broken algorithm, but the fix sent legitimate std calls through the hash partition — contradicting QEX Appendix A's invariant "28 bits are enough to encode any standard call sign uniquely" (and Table 7's explicit "Standard call signs" range `[6257896, 268435455]`).

   The spec-correct algorithm: pad the input call so its digit lands at field-position 3 (the 0-indexed third position in the 6-char canonical form). For "K1JT" (digit at input index 1, 1-char prefix) → " K1JT " (1 leading + 1 trailing space). For "G3X" → " G3X  ". For "AB1CD" (5-char-2-prefix, digit at input index 2) → "AB1CD ". For "VK7MO" → "VK7MO ". With this alignment every per-position alphabet lookup succeeds non-negatively and n28 lands in `[stdCallOffset, 2^28)`. The reference `std_call_to_c28.f90` is incomplete (only handles 5-char-1-prefix and 6-char-2-prefix shapes); the paper text is the spec, not the reference program's gap.

   Implementation: `CallsignC28` now uses `stdCallPrefixLen(call)` (a refactor of `isStdCallsignShape` that returns 1 or 2 instead of bool) to determine digit position, then pads accordingly. `C28ToCallsign`'s recovery now `TrimSpace`-s both sides (was `TrimLeft`-only — digit-aligned padding can be on either side). `stdCallToC28` and `isLongFormatStdCallsign` dropped; their call sites in `encodeStd` (via `type1CallToC28`) and `encodeEUVHFP` go directly to `CallsignC28`. `isLetter`/`isDigit` helpers (only used by `isLongFormatStdCallsign`) also dropped.

   Regression tests cite QEX Appendix A Table 7 in failure messages: `TestCallsignC28_AllStdShapesLandInStdRange` enumerates every shape; `TestCallsignC28_PropertyAllStdShapesInStdRange` generates 5,000 random std-shape callsigns and pins all land in `[stdCallOffset, 2^28)`; `TestDecodeMessage_ShortStdCallRoundTrips` pins K1JT/G3X/M1A/VK7MO/AB1CD round-trip via Encode→Decode without hash-table state; `TestDecodeMessage_HashRangeC28StillNeedsLookup` preserves the legit "non-std call via Type 4 c58 → later h22 reference in Type 1 c28" path. Spec-vectors regenerated: M1A (was 6,050,834 → 10,608,568), K1JT (was 6,040,944 → 10,222,009), VK7MO (was 12,339,580 negative-index byproduct → 237,090,319 spec-correct); added G3X (9,483,721) and AB1CD (86,389,684). Phase 2C's `TestStdCallToC28_RoutingBasedOnShape` and `TestStdCallToC28_K1JTUsesActualHash` deleted.

3. **Finding #2 — Type 2 c28 must accept tokens (CQ / DE / QRZ / "CQ <suffix>").** Phase 3B's `validateType2Call` rejected all tokens. QEX Table 2 says the c28 field carries "Standard callsign, CQ, DE, QRZ, or 22-bit hash" universally; Table 1 rows 1 and 2 both use full c28 in both call slots. "CQ G4ABC/P JO22" is a valid Type 2 message.

   Fix: `validateType2Call` delegates to `validateType1Call`. New `validateType2Suffix` mirrors `validateType1Suffix` — rejects /P portable on a token. `encodeEUVHFP` uses `type1CallToC28` (token-aware) and invokes both suffix gates. `decodeEUVHFP` uses `type1CallFromC28`; obsolete `type2CallFromC28` removed. `formatEUVHFP` invokes the same gates. `parseEUVHFP` refactored to dispatcher shape mirroring `parseStd`: `parseCQEUVHFP` / `parseDirectedEUVHFP` / `parsePlainEUVHFP`. `isType1TokenStart` carve-out deleted.

   Tests cite QEX Table 2: `TestEncodeMessage_Type2_AcceptsToken` (was `_RejectsToken`); `TestDecodeMessage_Type2_AcceptsTokenInWire` (was `_RejectsTokenInWire`); `TestFormatMessage_Type2_RendersToken` (was `_RejectsToken`); `TestParseMessage_Type2_AcceptsTokenStart` (was `_RejectsTokenStart`); plus `_RejectsSuffixOnToken` for the /P-on-token gate. `TestType2_TextRoundTrip` extended with 7 token-prefixed cases.

4. **Finding #3 — Free Text parser must accept inputs without `.` or `?`.** Phase 3A's "design choice #3" required `.`/`?` as the eager trigger AND rejected fallback parsing. But QEX Table 1 canonical Type 0.0 example "TNX BOB 73 GL" has neither character — strict-or-error rejected the paper's own example.

   Fix: after structured dispatch, `parseStd(tokens)` is tried; if it fails AND `validateFreeText(trimmed)` accepts the input (≤ 13 chars, all chars in f71 alphabet), `parseFreeText(trimmed)` runs as fallback. The eager `.`/`?` trigger is unchanged for inputs that have those marker chars.

   Tests: `TestParseMessage_FreeText_NoTriggerFallback` (replacing `_NoTriggerStaysStructured`) pins "TNX BOB 73 GL", "HELLO", "73 OM", "FB 73", "CQ", "DE", "QRZ" → Type 0.0. `TestParseMessage_Rejects` cleaned up — only out-of-alphabet (`!`) and oversized (> 13 chars) cases remain. `TestFormatParse_RoundTrip` extended with 4 no-trigger Free Text inputs.

5. **Finding #4 — Type 5 decode must not panic on out-of-range g25.** 25-bit g25 has 33,554,432 codepoints; only 18,662,400 (≈56%) map to valid 6-char Maidenhead. `G25ToGrid6` panicked on out-of-range, crashing any caller that decoded untrusted bytes.

   Fix: `G25ToGrid6` signature changed from `(uint32) string` to `(uint32) (string, bool)`. Out-of-range returns `("", false)`. New `ErrInvalidGrid6` sentinel; `decodeEUVHFHash` checks the bool and wraps with `fmt.Errorf("%w: g25=%d", ...)`.

   Tests: `TestG25ToGrid6_RejectsOutOfRange` covers maxGrid6 + top of 25-bit + mid-range invalid; `TestDecodeMessage_Type5_RejectsInvalidGrid6` builds a Type 5 wire body with g25=maxGrid6, wraps in `defer recover()`, asserts `errors.Is(err, ErrInvalidGrid6)`.

6. **Type 3 RTTY Roundup SHIPPED end-to-end** on the corrected foundation:
   - **`wire.go`** — `i3RTTYRoundup = 3`, `t1Bits = 1`, `s13Bits = 13`, `s13SerialMax = 7999`, `s13StateBase = 8001`, `r3DisplayBiasType3 = 2` (per QEX Table 2 r3 row "529 ... 599 (type 3)"; r3=0 → "529", r3=7 → "599").
   - **`rttyroundup.go` (new file)** — Layer 1 multi-modal s13 primitive. `rttyRoundupStates` table verbatim from QEX ref [14] `states_provinces.txt` (65 entries). `S13Kind` enum: `Unknown / Serial / State / Unassigned`. `SerialToS13` / `StateToS13` forwards. `S13ToExchange(uint16) (serial uint16, state string, kind S13Kind)` inverse.
   - **`message.go`** — added `TU bool` (t1 prefix) and `StateProvince string` (state-form exchange). `Serial` reused (Type 5 bounds 2047; Type 3 bounds 7999 via per-Type validator).
   - **`encode.go`** — `encodeRTTYRoundup` packs `t1 c28 c28 R1 r3 s13 i3=3 = 77 bits`. Token-aware c28 via `type1CallToC28`. Validates Call1/Call2 (`validateType1Call`), Report3 ∈ [0,7] (new `validateRTTYReport`), exclusive Serial/StateProvince choice.
   - **`decode.go`** — `decodeRTTYRoundup` inverse; routes c28 via `type1CallFromC28`; uses `S13ToExchange` to populate either Serial or StateProvince; new `ErrInvalidS13` for unassigned s13 codepoints (8000, > 8065) — same panic-to-error pattern as finding #4.
   - **`format.go`** — `formatRTTYRoundup` renders `"[TU; ]<call1> <call2> [R ]5N9 <exchange>"` with 4-digit zero-padded serial or state code.
   - **`parse.go`** — `parseRTTYRoundup` handles all shapes (TU prefix, R ack, token-aware Call1, digit-or-state exchange). `isType3Trigger` fires on `"TU;"` first-token OR `"5N9"` 3-digit report token (N ∈ 2..9). Dispatched between Type 2 and Type 1.
   - **Tests:** 4 new test files, ~400 lines: `rttyroundup_test.go` (Layer 1 — 6 tests), `type3_test.go` (Layer 2 — wire layout, i3=3 tag pin, encode rejects, round-trip across serial/state/TU/ack/token-in-Call1/table-boundary cases, invalid-s13 panic-to-error pin), `type3_format_test.go` (format basic shapes 12 cases, format rejects, parse basic shapes 13 cases, parse rejects, text round-trip 14 cases). Plus i3=3 added to `decode_test.go` dispatch-skip list; `MessageTypeRTTYRU` removed from `encode_test.go`'s "unsupported" expectation.

### Session 76 (2026-05-20) — Phase 4 receiver-side hash table SHIPPED

Phase 4 kicks off with the **infrastructure piece** Phase 3 deferred: the receiver-side running callsign-hash table per QEX paper §6. Type 4 (NonStd Call) and Type 5 (EU VHF hashes+g25) decoders already surface `<...>` sentinels + raw `Hash12`/`Hash22` values; the table closes the loop so a Resolve pass can replace those sentinels with the callsign strings the receiver has seen on the band recently.

**What shipped (one file, one test file):**

1. **`internal/ft8/codec/hashtable.go` (new).** `HashTable` struct with bounded capacity (`DefaultHashTableCapacity = 100`, the WSJT-X convention), thread-safe via `sync.RWMutex`. Storage is a flat `[]hashEntry` slice — oldest at `[0]`, newest at `[len-1]` — chosen over three reverse-index maps because at N=100 the linear scan is trivial (µs-scale) and the data structure is dead-simple to reason about. Each entry carries the callsign string + precomputed `h10`/`h12`/`h22` so lookups don't re-run HashCodes per entry.

2. **`Insert(callsign string)`.** Trims whitespace (HashCodes treats trailing space as a shorter call — without trimming, "K1JT" and "K1JT " would hash identically but store as two strings). Silently filters non-callsigns via `isInsertableCallsign`: rejects empty, the `"<...>"` sentinel, anything `TokenToC28` recognises (CQ / DE / QRZ / `CQ NNN` / `CQ <suffix>`), strings longer than `hashCallsignLen` (11), and any character outside `hashAlphabet`. If the callsign is already present, it's moved to the most-recent slot (LRU touch); otherwise appended and the oldest entry is dropped if over capacity.

3. **`LookupH22(uint32) (string, bool)` / `LookupH12(uint16) (string, bool)` / `LookupH10(uint16) (string, bool)`.** Each scans newest-to-oldest so the most recently inserted call wins on hash collision. Collision rates at cap=100 are ≈0.002% / 2.4% / 10% — h10 collisions are common in practice but h10 is only consulted by Type 0.x specialty messages.

4. **`Observe(m Message)`.** Walks `Call1`/`Call2` and Inserts each. No per-Type dispatch needed — Insert's filter handles tokens (CQ slot in Type 1) and sentinels (hashed side in Types 4/5), so a single Observe call works for every decoded Message shape. Suffix bits (`/R`, `/P`) are not part of `Call1`/`Call2` (they're separate fields), so the bare callsign is what gets stored — matches how HashCodes is invoked everywhere else in the codec.

5. **`Resolve(m Message) Message`.** Returns a copy of `m` with sentinel call slots replaced by table lookups. Per-Type behavior:
   - **Type 4 (NonStd Call)** — one hash slot. Whichever of `Call1`/`Call2` is the sentinel is resolved via `Hash12`; the other side stays as-is.
   - **Type 5 (EU VHF hashes+g25)** — both call slots are sentinels. `Call1` resolves via `Hash12`, `Call2` via `Hash22`.
   - **Other Types** — returned unchanged (Type 1/2/0.0 carry no sentinel slots in the current codec; Type 1's hash-partition c28 still errors at decode time, see deferred follow-up below).
   On successful resolution the corresponding `Hash12`/`Hash22` is zeroed so a downstream observer can't tell a hash-resolved call from a natively-plaintext one. If the table doesn't yet hold the call for a given hash, that slot stays as the sentinel and the Hash field stays non-zero — the caller can retry after more Observe calls populate the table.

6. **`Len() int`** for tests and instrumentation.

7. **`hashtable_test.go` (new, 16 tests, all passing):**
   - `TestNewHashTable_DefaultCapacity` / `TestNewHashTable_CustomCapacity` — capacity fallback on non-positive input + explicit cap respected.
   - `TestHashTable_InsertLookup_HappyPath` — insert a real call (`PJ4/K1ABC` for `/`-alphabet coverage), look it up via all three widths.
   - `TestHashTable_Lookup_Miss` — return `("", false)` on unused hash, not a stale entry.
   - `TestHashTable_Insert_FiltersJunk` — empty / sentinel / tokens (CQ, DE, QRZ, `CQ DX`, `CQ POTA`, `CQ 123`) / lowercase / punctuation / > 11 chars all silently skipped.
   - `TestHashTable_Insert_TrimsWhitespace` — `"  K1JT  "` lands as `"K1JT"`, no duplicate row.
   - `TestHashTable_Insert_LRUOnReinsert` — reinsert moves to MRU; verified via direct `entries` inspection so the ordering rule stays pinned.
   - `TestHashTable_FIFOEvictionAtCapacity` — capacity-3 table, 5 inserts; oldest 2 evicted.
   - `TestHashTable_Observe_PopulatesFromCallSlots` — Type 1 message inserts both sides; Call1=CQ inserts only the non-token side.
   - `TestHashTable_Observe_SkipsSentinels` — Type 4 with `<...>` Call1 inserts only Call2.
   - `TestHashTable_Resolve_Type4_Call1Sentinel` / `TestHashTable_Resolve_Type4_Call2Sentinel` — both h1 branches.
   - `TestHashTable_Resolve_Type5_BothSentinels` — happy path, both call slots resolve.
   - `TestHashTable_Resolve_Type5_PartialResolution` — Call1 resolves, Call2 unknown; sentinel + Hash22 preserved for retry.
   - `TestHashTable_Resolve_EmptyTable` — input untouched on cold table.
   - `TestHashTable_Resolve_NonHashType_Untouched` — Types 1/2/0.0 round-trip unchanged.

**Verified:** `go build ./...` clean, `go vet ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/ft8/codec/ -race` green (full codec suite + new tests), `go test ./...` green.

**Deferred follow-up (NOT shipped this session):** Type 1's `decodeStd` still returns `ErrCallsignNeedsHashLookup` when a c28 lands in the hash partition (`[nTokens, stdCallOffset)`). To make Type 1 short-call decode symmetric with Type 4/5, the path would surface `Call1=<...>` (or `Call2=<...>`) + populate `Hash22`, letting `Resolve` handle it the same way. The `LookupH22` primitive is in place when that work lands. Not done this turn because (a) the user asked specifically for the hash table, not the decoder shape change; (b) Type 1 has only one Hash22 field for two possible hash sides — the convention "sentinel slot identifies which Hash22 applies" works but is worth pinning in a follow-up Step.

**Design notes worth pinning (memory):**

1. **Flat slice beat three reverse-index maps for the hash table.** Linear scan at N=100 is microseconds; the alternative (one map per hash width with collision-cascade eviction) is significantly more complex for no measurable runtime benefit at the target scale. "Build specific, not generic" applies — the constant factor only matters at 10k+ entries, which the WSJT-X cap of 100 is nowhere near.

2. **Insert's silent-filter contract.** Observe calls Insert on every Call slot regardless of Type. Insert filters tokens / sentinels / out-of-alphabet silently rather than erroring because the caller can't sensibly recover from "this slot wasn't a real callsign" — it's the expected shape on every QSO. Making Insert return an error would just turn into mandatory `_ = ht.Insert(...)` at every call site.

3. **Resolve zeroes the Hash field on success.** Two reasons: (a) prevents accidental re-resolution if Resolve is called twice; (b) makes a resolved Message structurally identical to one that decoded plaintext directly, so downstream code doesn't need to know about the provenance.

4. **Newest-wins on collision via newest-to-oldest iteration.** WSJT-X's documented behavior. The older colliding entry stays in the table and remains reachable via its non-colliding hashes (h22 collision doesn't imply h12 collision), but lookups for the colliding hash always return the freshest call. This matches the operator mental model: "the call I just heard wins."

**Next:** Phase 4 has four remaining pieces in scope: Type 0.1 (DXpedition), Type 0.3 (Field Day ARRL), Type 0.4 (Field Day RAC), Type 0.5 (Telemetry), all in the i3=0 family (n3 sub-dispatch is already wired — current decoder errors with `ErrUnknownMessageType: i3=0 n3=N` for n3 ∈ {1, 3, 4, 5}). Plus Type 3 (RTTY Roundup) at i3=3 — wait, that's the same i3 as Type 5 EU VHF Hash. Let me re-verify against QEX Table 1 at start of next session — Type 3 may actually be i3=5, with Type 5 EU VHF Hash at i3=3 (the tag-to-Type mapping is not "Type N = i3=N"; it's a paper-labeling vs. wire-tag indirection that's bitten us before). Whatever the i3, Type 3 RTTY RU's wire shape is `c28 + r1 + c28 + r1 + R1 + r3 + s13 + i3` — same two-c28 shape as Types 1/2 with new `r3` (3-bit report, same as Type 5) + `s13` (13-bit serial, wider than Type 5's s11) fields. The receiver-side hash table from this session unblocks any of these whose decode surfaces a sentinel side.

After Phase 4, Layer 2 closes; the work moves to Layer 3 (LDPC decoder + Costas sync + FFT/demod signal-processing pipeline).

### Session 75 (2026-05-20) — Layer 2 Phase 3D SHIPPED (Type 5 EU VHF hashes+g25)

Phase 3D closes the fourth and final Phase-3 message type — Type 5 is the **contest-style EU VHF exchange** where BOTH callsigns hash to the wire (h12 + h22) and the rest of the message carries the ack bit + RST-style report + serial + 6-character grid. Wire layout: `h12 + h22 + R1 + r3 + s11 + g25 + i3=3` = 77 bits. Example from QEX Table 1: `<G4ABC> <PA9XYZ> R 570007 JO22DB`.

**What shipped:**

1. **Layer 1 inverse — `G25ToGrid6` in `grid.go`.** Base-(18,18,10,10,24,24) divmod from the right; pinned via round-trip test against `Grid6ToG25`. Out-of-range g25 panics (corrupted wire LDPC+CRC14 would catch). The grid slot has NO reserved-token or signed-report multiplexing (unlike g15), so every in-range value is a 6-char grid — no kind discriminator needed.

2. **Wire constants in `wire.go`.** New `i3EUVHFHash = 3` (Type 5 tag), `r3Bits = 3`, `s11Bits = 11`, `r3Bias = 52` (lifts raw 0..7 code to 2-digit display "52..59"), `s11Max = 2047`. Layer 1 widths (`HashBits22` in hashcodes.go, `G25Bits` in grid.go) stay with their primitive files per the established Phase 3C convention.

3. **`Message` struct extensions in `message.go`.** Four new fields: `Hash22 uint32` (paralleling Type 4's `Hash12`), `Report3 uint8` (0..7 raw code), `Serial uint16` (0..2047), `Grid6 string` (6-char Maidenhead — kept separate from the existing `Grid string` multi-modal g15 slot since g25 has different semantics). `Hash12`'s doc updated to cover both Type 4 and Type 5.

4. **Encoder — `encodeEUVHFHash` in `encode.go`.** Validates both calls as std-callsign-only (tokens rejected); hashes Call1 → h12, Call2 → h22; bounds-checks Report3, Serial, Grid6; assembles the 77-bit body. Four new validators (`validateType5Call` / `validateType5Report` / `validateType5Serial` / `validateType5Grid`) with field-tagged error messages.

5. **Decoder — `decodeEUVHFHash` in `decode.go`.** Both call slots surface as the `hashedCallSentinel` (`"<...>"`) with raw `Hash12`/`Hash22` populated; `G25ToGrid6` fully recovers `Grid6`; `AckBit`/`Report3`/`Serial` decode straight from the wire.

6. **Format — `formatEUVHFHash` in `format.go`.** Brackets BOTH calls (the wire hashes both sides; WSJT-X display convention always wraps); `renderType5Call` mirrors `renderType4Call`'s three-shape acceptance (sentinel, pre-bracketed, bare std → wrap). Report+serial fuse into one token (`57` + `0007` = `570007`).

7. **Parser — `parseEUVHFHash` in `parse.go`.** New `isType5Trigger` classifier helper: BOTH first two tokens angle-bracketed AND last token is a 6-char Maidenhead grid → Type 5. New `splitReportSerial` helper splits the fused body token. Free Text classifier was tightened — now requires absence of angle brackets — so the `<...>` sentinel's literal periods don't trip `.` → Free Text routing before structured classification runs. Final dispatch order: **Free Text (`./?` AND no `<>`) → Type 5 (dual `<>` + grid6 trailing) → Type 4 (any trigger) → Type 2 (`/P`) → Type 1.**

8. **Tests in new `type5_test.go`** (12 tests, all passing): layout pin against QEX Table 1, i3-tag-is-3 pin, encode rejections (9 cases), full Encode→Decode round-trip with `Hash12`/`Hash22` verification, format basic shapes, sentinel + pre-bracketed pass-through, format rejections, parse basic shapes (with lowercase normalisation), parse rejections, text→parse→encode→decode→format round-trip (sentinel-form output expected), classifier-order pin (Type 5 vs Type 4 boundary), `G25ToGrid6` Layer 1 round-trip.

Stale-test cleanup: `TestDecodeMessage_RejectsUnknownI3` skips i3=3; `TestEncodeMessage_UnsupportedType` drops `MessageTypeEUVHFHash`. All existing codec tests still pass; full `go test ./...` green; `go vet ./...` clean.

**Doc audit pass:** Bumped CLAUDE.md FT8 bullet + milestones.md M4.1 preamble + Layer 1 primitives table (`Grid6ToG25` row gains `G25ToGrid6` inverse) + Phase 2 additions table (new `encodeEUVHFHash` / `decodeEUVHFHash` rows; `Message` / `wire.go` / `Format` / `Parse` rows updated for Type 5 paths + tightened Free Text classifier), Memory project_ft8_library.md frontmatter + Layer 2 status section + new Phase 3D bullet, Memory MEMORY.md FT8 line.

**Design-pinning notes worth keeping (memory):**

1. **Free Text classifier needs to step out of the way of structured-message hashed-call display forms.** The `<...>` sentinel contains `.` which tripped the original `./?` trigger before structured classification could see the input. Fix: require absence of `<>` in the trigger condition. f71's alphabet excludes `<>` so any real Free Text input never has them; the asymmetry is one-way safe.

2. **Type 5 classifier trigger needs to be SHARPER than Type 4's.** Type 4 also has angle brackets (one side is hashed). Type 5 has TWO bracketed calls AND a 6-char Maidenhead grid at the trailing position — both are required. Dispatch-order: check Type 5 first, then fall through to Type 4 if either condition fails.

3. **Layer 1 inverses ship alongside Type-introduction milestones (continued from Phase 3C).** Phase 3D shipped `G25ToGrid6`; the pattern holds. Phase 4's specialty types may shift this — Type 0.5 Telemetry uses t71 which already has an inverse via the f71 family; Type 3 RTTY RU uses s13 (a different width from Type 5's s11) and may need a tiny helper, not a full primitive.

4. **Three distinct grid fields now exist on `Message` and that's OK.** `Grid string` is the multi-modal g15 slot (Type 1/2; can be 4-char grid, signed report, reserved token). `Grid6 string` is the strict 6-char g25 slot (Type 5). The structural difference is large enough that one field with a kind discriminator would be more confusing than two fields with type-specific semantics — the project rule "build specific, not generic" applies.

**Next:** **Phase 4 — specialty types (Type 0.1 DXpedition, Type 0.3/0.4 Field Day, Type 3 RTTY RU, Type 0.5 Telemetry) + receiver-side hash table.** Layer 2 closes after Phase 4 lands; signal-processing layers (LDPC decoder, FFT/sync/demod) start after that. Type 3 (RTTY RU) introduces s13 (different width from Type 5's s11); the other Phase-4 types are all in the i3=0 family (n3 sub-dispatch already wired). The hash table is the big infrastructure piece — a running map from 12/22-bit hash to most-recently-seen callsign, fed by every successful decode and consulted on the `<...>` sentinel paths of Types 4/5. Phase 4 design questions for the next Step A: where the hash table lives (codec package? FT8 service layer?); cache sizing + eviction; persistence (in-memory only? snapshot on shutdown?); how decode-side resolution surfaces in the API.

2. `git log --oneline -10` to see Session-75's commits.

### Session 74 (2026-05-20) — Layer 2 Phase 3C SHIPPED (Type 4 NonStd Call)

Three commits this session. Phase 3C closes the third of the four Phase-3 message types per the 3A→3B→3C→3D ordering. First message type whose wire shape breaks the c28+c28+g15 mould — Type 4's `h12 + c58 + h1 + r2 + c1 + i3=4` carries one 12-bit hash (referencing a std callsign via the receiver's Phase-4 hash table) + one 58-bit nonstandard callsign + a 2-bit r2 token slot + a 1-bit c1 "CQ-from-nonstd" flag.

**Phase 3C Step A — design sign-off (no code).** Four sign-off questions answered with my recommendations + a bonus rule:
1. Hash representation: reuse `Call1`/`Call2` strings + add a `Hash12 uint16` field (zero for resolved/encoded, non-zero only when decode hasn't resolved the hash to a callsign). Matches WSJT-X's `<...>` / `<W9XYZ>` display convention; minimal field churn.
2. Scope: encode + decode-stub (not encode-only). The c58 side is fully recoverable from the wire via `CallsignC58`'s inverse, so decode returns a partial-success Message with the nonstd side resolved + `Hash12` raw value + `<...>` sentinel on the hash side. Phase 4 fills the string in.
3. r2 token slot: reuse `Grid` field (constrained to `{"", "RRR", "RR73", "73"}`). Same value set as Type 1's g15 reserved tokens; the wire-width difference (2 bits vs 15) is an encoder/decoder concern, not a Message-layer one.
4. c1 CQ flag: implicit from `Call1 == "CQ"`. Encoder sets c1=1 when Call1=="CQ"; decoder sets Call1="CQ" when c1=1; no new bool field. Reject CQ-with-suffix (c1 is 1 bit, no room).
   Bonus rule: h1 (hash side) is implicit from std-vs-nonstd shape detection. Encoder errors on both-std (use Type 1) or both-nonstd (ambiguous coin-flip).

**Phase 3C Step B — Layer 1 inverse + Type 4 bit layer (committed).** First: `C58ToCallsign` Layer 1 inverse in `nonstdcall.go` — base-38 divmod from the right; trims trailing spaces per CallsignC58's left-justified padding; panics on c58 ≥ 2^58 (upper-bit guard). Round-trip tests against the existing nonstd_to_c58 spec vectors. New `Message.Hash12 uint16` field with doc on the `<...>` sentinel + Phase 4 resolution path. New `i3NonStdCall = 4` constant. New `encodeNonStdCall` packs `h12+c58+h1+r2+c1+i3=4` = 77 bits; std-vs-nonstd shape detection picks h1; `Call1=="CQ"` sets c1; `gridToR2`/`r2ToGrid` helpers map the 2-bit token slot. `validateType4Calls` enforces the shape rules + `isType4ValidNonStdCall` gates the c58 alphabet upstream of CallsignC58's panic path; CQ-with-suffix rejected via precedence-safe `strings.HasPrefix("CQ ")` check. `decodeNonStdCall` inverts the layout; new `type2CallFromC28`-style helper recovers nonstd via `C58ToCallsign`, fills `<...>` sentinel + `Hash12` on the hashed side. CQ-from-nonstd path (c1=1) zeros `Hash12` per spec. New `wire.go` centralises Layer 2 wire-format constants (`MessageBits` moved out of crc14.go, `i3Width`/`i3Offset` moved out of decode.go, all i3/n3/Type 4 widths + r2 codes consolidated). Tests in new `type4_test.go`: layout pin (4 shapes), i3-tag-is-4 pin, encode rejections (9 cases), full Encode→Decode round-trip (6 shapes covering both h1 orderings + CQ + all r2 tokens), r2 token slot pin (all 4 values), `<...>` sentinel pin, CQ-zero-hash pin, c58 alphabet acceptance, i3=4 dispatch sanity check. Stale-test cleanup: `TestDecodeMessage_RejectsUnknownI3` skips i3=4; `TestEncodeMessage_UnsupportedType` drops `MessageTypeNonStdCall`.

**Phase 3C Step C — text layer + classifier (committed).** `formatNonStdCall` renders Type 4 with angle brackets on the hashed side; `renderType4Call` accepts std-shape (encoder-input case, wraps), `"<...>"` sentinel (decoder-output unresolved, verbatim), pre-bracketed strings (decoder-output post-Phase-4-resolved, verbatim), `"CQ"` (verbatim), or nonstd-shape c58 calls (verbatim). Format-side validator is laxer than encode's (the encoder needs real strings to hash; the formatter just renders). `FormatMessage` dispatches `MessageTypeNonStdCall`; `TestFormatMessage_UnsupportedType` drops it. New `parseNonStdCall` strips outer angle brackets via `stripAngleBrackets` (passes the `<...>` sentinel through), validates the trailing token is in `{"", "RRR", "RR73", "73"}`, two-call slots in either order. New `isType4Trigger` classifier helper with three trigger conditions: (a) angle brackets present, (b) any token with `/` that isn't a Type 1 /R or Type 2 /P trailing suffix, (c) any token > 6 chars without slash (catches special-event calls like `YW18FIFA`). `ParseMessage` classifier dispatch order: Free Text (`./?`) → Type 4 (any trigger) → Type 2 (`/P` suffix) → Type 1; ordering matters because a compound nonstd ending in `/P` (e.g. `PJ4/K1ABC/P`) routes to Type 4 rather than Type 2 (Type 2's c28 partition is std-only). Tests: format basic shapes (6 cases), sentinel + pre-bracketed pass-through (4 cases), format rejections (6 cases), parse basic shapes (7 cases with lowercase normalisation), parse rejections (4 cases), full text→parse→encode→decode→format round-trip pinning the sentinel-form output, classifier-order pin (8 cases covering all four trigger types).

**Design-pinning notes worth keeping (memory):**

1. **Layer 1 inverses ship alongside Type-introduction milestones, not as a separate phase.** Originally I expected Phase 3C to be Type 4 work only — landed up shipping `C58ToCallsign` as part of Step B because the decode path needs it. The pattern: each new message type whose decode-side recovers a string slot drives the corresponding Layer 1 inverse. Type 5 (Phase 3D) won't need a new Layer 1 inverse — it uses h12 + h22 + g25 wire fields where h22/h12 are already hash codes (decoded to sentinels) and g25 has `Grid6ToG25` whose inverse we'll need (write it in Phase 3D Step B alongside the Type 5 work).
2. **wire.go centralisation is the long-term home for Layer 2 wire-format constants.** Per-primitive Layer 1 widths stay with their primitive files (they belong to the primitive's algorithm). i3 tags / n3 family / per-Type widths / per-Type token codes are the shared invariants between encode and decode — they live in wire.go.
3. **Format-side validators are laxer than encode-side validators when decode-output shapes can't be encoded.** Type 1/2's format validators share the same gate as encode (any Message that round-trips through one round-trips through the other). Type 4 breaks this: a decoded Message with `Call1 = "<...>"` formats fine but can't encode (no string to hash). The asymmetry captures the actual lifecycle — Phase 4's hash table resolves the sentinel before any re-encode.
4. **Classifier triggers stay sharp and unambiguous.** Each Type's trigger char/pattern is in NO other Type's alphabet: `./?` unique to f71; `/P` unique to Type 2's wire bit (Type 1 uses /R); angle brackets, mid-slash, non-/R-non-/P trailing slash, and length > 6 are all Type 4 signals. Mixed cases (e.g. compound nonstd ending in /P) resolve to the more-specific Type 4 because the classifier checks in spec-tightness order (Free Text → Type 4 → Type 2 → Type 1).

**Next:** **Phase 3D — Type 5 EU VHF hashes+g25.** Wire shape per QEX Table 1: `h12 h22 R1 r3 s11 g25`. Two hashed callsigns (h12 + h22 widths), an R1 ack bit, a 3-bit r3 RST report range, an 11-bit s11 serial number, and a 6-character g25 Maidenhead grid (vs Types 1/2's 4-character g15). Example: `<G4ABC> <PA9XYZ> R 570007 JO22DB`. Requires shipping `Grid6ToG25` Layer 1 inverse (the forward is already in `grid.go`). Both call slots decode to `<...>` sentinels + raw h12/h22 values; Phase 4's hash table resolves. New `Message.Hash22` field (already implied by h22 width — currently `Hash12 uint16` covers the 12-bit case; either widen to `Hash22 uint32` or add a separate field per side). Step A's design questions: hash representation (one or two new fields?); serial / RST representation in Message; whether to ship Phase 3D Step B with Grid6ToG25 inverse + encoder, leave decoder for Phase 4 because both hashes are unresolved, or ship the full encode+decode-stub like 3C did.

New Phase 3B tests in `euvhfp_test.go`: Type 2 format pin (10 shape vectors covering plain pair, suffix per-call, both suffix, report, ack patterns, reserved tokens), Type 2 format token-rejection pin, Type 2 parse pin (9 dispatch cases including lowercase normalisation), mixed `/R + /P` rejection (3 cases), Type 1 token-start rejection (4 cases including `CQ DX G4ABC/P JO22`), full text→parse→encode→decode→format round-trip suite (9 inputs).

**Doc audit pass (this entry, plus the changes shipped this session).** Bumped CLAUDE.md line 8 status, milestones.md M4.1 preamble + Phase 2 additions table (new rows for encodeEUVHFP / decodeEUVHFP and updates to the Message / Format / Parse rows reflecting Type 2 paths + Suffix rename), Memory project_ft8_library.md frontmatter + Layer 2 status section, Memory MEMORY.md FT8 line.

**Design-pinning notes worth keeping (memory):**

1. **Type 2 forks Type 1 rather than parametrising.** Every layer has genuine per-type behaviour — the parametrised path would accumulate knobs (i3 tag, allow-tokens, suffix char) and the memory rule "build specific, not generic; three specific implementations are easier to read than one clever abstraction" applies. If Types 3/0.3/0.4 (which also use a c28+c28+R1+payload shape) end up sharing meaningful structure with Type 1/Type 2, that's the right moment to extract a shared helper — not now on speculation.
2. **Classifier triggers are unambiguous chars.** `.` / `?` are unique to f71. `/P` is unique to Type 2 (Type 1 uses `/R`). The pre-scan stays cheap (one HasSuffix per token) and keeps each parser single-Type. When Type 4 (NonStd Call) lands in Phase 3C, the trigger will be `<` / `>` (the angle-bracket hash-syntax per QEX paper) — also unique, also detectable upfront.
3. **Bit slot is single-Type per message.** A single message can't mix `/R` and `/P` on its two callsigns — the wire bit at offset 28/57 means r1 OR p1 depending on i3, not both. `consumePortableCall` enforces this at parse time with an explicit mixed-Type error.

**Next:** **Phase 3C — Type 4 NonStd Call.** Structurally different from Types 1/2: uses the c58 partition (compound/special-event callsigns up to 11 chars) + a 22-bit hash slot for the other call, plus a small payload (R1 + r2/RRR token). Wire shape per QEX Table 1: `h12 c58 h1 r2 c1`. The c58 primitive (`CallsignC58`) is already shipped at Layer 1. Open questions for Step A: how to represent the hash-vs-recovered-call asymmetry in the Message struct (separate field, or overload Call1/Call2 with a "this side is a 22-bit hash" sentinel?); whether the receiver-side 22-bit hash lookup (Phase 4) blocks Phase 3C, or whether Phase 3C lands the encode-side first and decode surfaces `ErrCallsignNeedsHashLookup` until Phase 4 wires the table.

Three round-trip tests, layout pin (n3/i3 bit positions), bad-input rejection (7 validation cases), n3 sub-dispatch test (all 8 n3 values). Layer 1 inverse spec vectors round-trip all 8 existing reference-program vectors plus 17 round-trip inputs.

**Phase 3A Step C — `FormatMessage` / `ParseMessage` text layer + classifier (committed).** `formatFreeText` emits `m.FreeText` as-is (validation reuses `validateFreeText` so format/encode reject the same things). `ParseMessage` reshaped: empty-check first, then classifier — presence of `.` or `?` (chars unique to f71, not in std-callsign / signed-report / rover alphabets) routes to `parseFreeText`; otherwise tokenise via `strings.Fields` and route to `parseStd`. `parseFreeText` validates via the same `validateFreeText` gate. Format tests: 5 shape vectors + 4 bad-input cases. Parse tests: 7 dispatch cases (period/question alone, with spaces, max length, whitespace trimming, lowercase normalisation, structured-shape-with-trigger) + length-boundary rejection + 3 no-trigger-stays-structured rejections. Headline `TestFormatParse_RoundTrip` extended with 5 Free Text cases (`"HELLO."` / `"73 OM."` / `"TNX BOB 73."` / `"WHAT?"` / `"K1JT?"`) — full text→parse→encode→decode→format→encode chain bit-for-bit AND text-for-text.

**One design-pinning note worth keeping:** the classifier rule is "`.` or `?` ⇒ Free Text dispatch". This is sharper than the design proposal mentioned ("chars outside std-callsign alphabet"). The reason: `+` / `-` / `/` are in BOTH alphabets (used in signed reports and `/R` rover suffix in structured parsing). Only `.` and `?` are unambiguous f71-only triggers. If the dispatcher saw `+` or `-` and routed to Free Text, structured signed reports would break. Test cases pin both branches.

Fixed with `reportMin/reportMax` constants and a new test `report_below_protocol_range`; also caught "eight"→"ten" doc typo, sentinel-text wording, and the choice to migrate to `internal/errors` for tagged errors while keeping the sentinel on stdlib `errors.New`.

**4. QEX paper deep-read mid-Phase-2C revealed the short-callsign protocol quirk.** I had to fetch the QEX paper locally (`/home/mveary/Downloads/FT4_FT8_QEX.pdf`) to settle the inverse-arithmetic question; Appendix A doesn't spell out an inverse algorithm. Running the Fortran reference `std_call_to_c28` against `K1JT` and `A1JT` confirmed they produce **identical** c28 = 6040944 — the forward algorithm's negative-index trick (for chars right-padded into positions where the per-position alphabet doesn't accept them) deliberately collapses 4-char-1-prefix calls onto the same code points. Similarly `AB1CD`, `AB2CD`, `AB9CD` all collapse to c28 = 8205869 (5-char-2-prefix calls collide on the digit). The protocol disambiguates these via the receiver's 22-bit hash table — which means `CallsignC28` is NOT a function the encoder should call for short callsigns. The correct encoding for K1JT in a Type 1 slot is `HashedCallC28("K1JT") = 4159881`, the call's real 22-bit hash + nTokens bias. This finding amended Phase 2C's scope to include an encoder routing fix.

**5. Phase 2C — Layer 1 inverses + Type 1 decoder + encoder routing fix + round-trip suite (commit da720d7).** Five threads in one commit:

- **Layer 1 inverse `C28ToCallsign(c28) (string, C28Kind)`** in `callsign.go`. Route-B kind enum: `C28KindUnknown` / `C28KindToken` (c28 < nTokens) / `C28KindHash22` (c28 in hash partition) / `C28KindStdCall` (c28 in std partition). Only `StdCall` returns a non-empty string; `Token` and `Hash22` callers need additional state (token table, 22-bit hash table). The std-call inverse is a straight unshifted mixed-base divmod — my earlier algebra worried about needing a shift trick but careful re-verification showed std-call partition guarantees all forward indices ≥ 0, so the divmod recovers them directly.
- **Layer 1 inverse `G15ToGrid4(g15) (string, G15Kind)`** in `grid.go`. Kind enum: `Unknown` / `Grid4` / `Reserved` / `Report`. All three populated kinds return a meaningful string ("FN20" / "RR73" / "+02"). Decoder canonicalises reports to the 2-digit form (`formatSignedReport` — matches WSJT-X display convention). Wire-input asymmetry documented: g15 == maxGrid4 decodes to "-35" (outside protocol band) — Grid4ToG15 never produces this value but a corrupted wire decode could.
- **Phase 2B encoder routing fix** — new `stdCallToC28(call)` dispatch in `encode.go`. Long-format std calls (5-char-1-prefix `[letter][digit][letter]{3}` like G4ABC; 6-char-2-prefix `[alnum]{2}≥1-letter[digit][letter]{3}` like AB1CDE / 2E0XYZ) go through `CallsignC28`. Everything else (3-char, 4-char, 5-char-2-prefix like VK7MO/AB1CD) goes through `HashedCallC28`. Test pins both that K1JT now encodes to 4159881 (the right hash) AND that it does NOT encode to 6040944 (the negative-index byproduct — regression guard).

### Session 68 (2026-05-17) — FT8 milestone scope + GPL/MIT licensing constraint pinned

Design pass, no code changes. Two intertwined outcomes: M4 milestones scoped into `milestones.md`, and the GPL v3 (WSJT-X) vs MIT (SM) licence gap surfaced and codified as a load-bearing constraint. The constraint revised the implementation source-of-truth from "Fortran sources" to "published protocol specs" — line-by-line translation of GPL source produces derivative work even across languages, which would force-relicense SM. The course correction landed alongside the milestones in the same session, before any FT8 implementation code goes near the repo.

**Survey done first:** distro `jt9` is installed at `/usr/bin/jt9` from the Fedora `wsjtx` package (`rpm -V` confirms unmodified install; signed by Fedora's key; license = GPL-3.0-or-later). The packaged binary works as the parity oracle without needing to build any upstream source. WSJT-X's source distribution is GPL v3 throughout.

**Added:** `## Milestone 4 — FT8 subsystem` in `docs/v2-design/milestones.md`, structured like M3a (design preamble + six sub-milestones each with status/scope/acceptance):

- **Design preamble** captures (in this order): **Licensing constraint** at the top (the load-bearing rule below); **Implementation source = published academic specs** (Joe Taylor's QEX July/August 2020 paper "The FT4 and FT8 Communication Protocols" + Steve Franke's companion papers + WSJT-X user docs — those give the LDPC(174,91) generator matrix, Costas sync sequence, symbol mapping, frame structure); **CGO committed** for permissively-licensed C deps only — KissFFT or PocketFFT (BSD-3) for FFT (**FFTW3 excluded** for being GPL v2 even though WSJT-X uses it), PortAudio (MIT-equivalent) leaning for audio, decided in M4.2; **`jt9` as black-box parity oracle**; package boundary inherited from ADR 0021 (ft8 may consume `qsoservice`/`cat`/`serial`; mustn't import bridge; bridge mustn't import ft8 — boundary tests already in place).
- **Defaults stated** for the four open questions so they don't block writing code: single-threaded implementation first (concurrency only if M4.2 measurements demand it); in-memory ring buffer for decoded messages (historical "who did I hear" is logbook-app scope per the `feedback_logging_vs_logbook_scope` memory); NTP-correct host assumed with slot-offset surfaced as status (no active clock correction in v1); TX (M4.4) explicitly blocked on the inbound CAT command path landing.
- **M4.1** — WAV-file decode, parity with `jt9 -8`. Smallest end-to-end slice; CI parity gate against an operator-supplied corpus via `$FT8_TEST_CORPUS` (no WAVs in repo per the licensing constraint); CI skips gracefully when oracle unavailable.
- **M4.2** — Continuous live audio + 15s slot scheduling aligned to UTC; `GET /v1/ft8/status` exposes slot-offset metric.
- **M4.3** — Rig-aware decode (read-only). Decodes tagged with band + dial freq; cross-subsystem signalling via a neutral pubsub package (leaning) rather than direct bridge↔ft8 import.
- **M4.4** — TX path (manual send). Blocked on inbound CAT command path.
- **M4.5** — QSO state machine (auto-sequencing CQ → reply → RR73 → 73); completed QSOs land via `qsoservice.Submit`; SSE event stream at `/v1/ft8/events`.
- **M4.6** — SPA panel for live decode list + click-to-call + in-progress QSO indicator.

**Licensing rules (load-bearing for all M4 work):**

- **Implementation source = published academic specs**, not the Fortran. WSJT-X source files (`*.f90`, `*.cpp`, `*.h`) are off-limits as implementation reference, regardless of where any local checkout happens to live.
- **WSJT-X binaries (`jt9`, `ft8sim`) are tools we exec for testing.** Tool use doesn't infect callers; same legal shape as compiling with GCC. The M4.1 parity gate operates entirely at this level.
- **No WSJT-X assets bundled in SM repo.** Test corpus is operator-supplied locally; CI skips parity tests when neither `jt9` nor the corpus is configured on the host.
- **CGO dependencies must be permissively licensed.** FFTW3 excluded (GPL v2); KissFFT or PocketFFT (BSD-3) replace it. PortAudio (MIT-equivalent) stays. Any future CGO dep gets its licence checked before vendoring.
- **Mathematical constants** (Costas array, LDPC parity matrix, CRC14 polynomial) are facts; cite the paper, don't copy a Fortran array literal byte-for-byte.
